 In defence of the RBI’s calibrated tightening 
 Central banks are rarely accused of moving too soon. Yet on October 7, the RBI raised the policy repo rate by 25 basis points to 5.50 per cent and adopted a stance of calibrated tightening.
 SANKALPA BHATTACHARJEE | New Delhi | October 27, 2026 8:51 am 
 15 April 2020 
 8 mins read -->
 -->
 -->
 File Photo: IANS 
 Central banks are rarely accused of moving too soon. Yet on October 7, the RBI raised the policy repo rate by 25 basis points to 5.50 per cent and adopted a stance of calibrated tightening. The release of the MPC meeting minutes on October 21 reveals that, while the rate decision was unanimous, two members preferred to maintain a neutral stance. By reversing course within two months and declaring that rate cuts are off the table, the RBI has chosen to stay ahead of the cycle rather than trail it. 
 The critics charge that RBI is fighting a supply shock that interest rates cannot cure. They are right about the cure but wrong about the counterfactual, since everything around the policy stance had already been repriced. Q1 FY27 delivered real GDP growth of 7.8 per cent on a nominal expansion of 10.3 per cent, with real GVA up 8.2 per cent. The expansion was broad-based: services grew 10 per cent, capital formation 11.9 per cent, manufacturing 9.2 per cent, and construction 7.7 per cent. The RBI accordingly lifted its FY27 growth forecast to 7.1 per cent. Credit tells a similar story with bank lending up 18.1 per cent against a deposit growth of 17.3 per cent. An economy this buoyant does not need cheap money, and the case for leniency weakens precisely when price pressures build. The immediate pressures are supply-driven. 
 Advertisement
 The monsoon ended 12.6 per cent below normal, with a strong El Niño expected through year-end. The Indian crude basket rose 42 per cent between July and September, to $116.1 a barrel, and October’s average so far is $120.3. An RBI staff study puts pass-through at about 20 basis points of headline inflation per 10 per cent rise. The rupee, 8 per cent weaker than a year ago, compounds the bill. Retail inflation , on the new 2024=100 series, reached 5.54 per cent in September; wholesale inflation exceeded 9.75 per cent for five consecutive months, with fuel and power at 25.85. Core inflation rose to 4.2 per cent from 3.9, and the RBI projects 4.4 per cent for the year. 
 Advertisement 
 Households are pricing it in: the R B I ’s September survey yours one-year-ahead expectations at 10.0 per cent, from 8.7 a year ago, and three-month expectations at 9.9, from 8.1. Medians overstate realised inflation, so the direction matters more. A supply shock hardens into persistence only when priced into wages and contracts, and expectations decide that. Policy must respond. With CPI projected at 5.2 per cent this fiscal, a 5.25 per cent repo rate left the real rate near zero; at 5.50 it is about 0.3. Against the 5.8 per cent the MPC expects over the next three quarters, it is still slightly negative. The Taylor rule offers a yardstick: a 2 per cent real rate, plus inflation, plus half the inflation gap (ignoring the output gap). 
 With inflation at 5.2 per cent against the target of 4, the rule gives 7.8 per cent. At 5.50 per cent, the RBI remains well below the rule, so the hike restores a cushion, not a constraint. India is not tightening alone. The ECB has raised its deposit rate twice since June, by a cumulative 50 basis points to 2.50 per cent; the Fed lifted its range to 3.75-4.00 per cent on Septemb er 16. Markets had already repriced: the 10-year G -sec par yield rose from 6.60 per cent in September 2025 to 7.14 by September 25; the 364-day T-bill yield, at 6.09, sat 84 basis points above the repo rate; the rupee fell from 88.72 to 95.89 per dollar, and the US 10-year yield reached 5.31 per cent on October 5. 
 The hike restores the 150-basis-point gap over the Fed’s upper bound that had shrunk to 125 after September 16, while FCNR(B) deposits supplied almost 93 per cent of the $143.6 billion raised through the swap window. The policy rate, thus, was the laggard of financial conditions, not their instigator. Borrowers on repo-linked floating loans will pay more: on an illustrative Rs 50 lakh, 20-year loan at 8.5 per cent, a quarter-point lifts the EMI from about Rs 43,400 to Rs 44,200, or roughly Rs 800 a month. Savers, however, earn 2.50 per cent on savings deposits against 4.8 per cent inflation, a real return of minus 2.3 points; term deposits above a year pay 6 to 6.75 per cent. The hike’s cost to borrowers is modest and visible; inflation’s cost to savers is larger and silent, and the stance guards against the greater burden. 
 Calibrated tightening commits the Committee to a direction, not a destination: in the near term, the next move is a hike or a pause, never a cut, and its depth follows the data. That is the right design for a shock whose duration nobody knows. If rains return, oil retreats, and expectations stabilise, the RBI pauses; if not, it has preserved the option to act again. The calendar will test this soon: the Fed meets on October 27-28, October inflation is due on November 12, and the MPC meets again from December 2 to 4. The most dangerous central bank is not the one that ac tbefore every doubt has disappeared, but the one that waits for certainty and discovers that the price of delay is far greater than the cost of timely action. 
 (The writer teaches Economics at IIM Ranchi. Views are personal.)
